e-5616.problem:
Consider the linear transformation 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071281/assets/c3d64ddcfd33db2e96caf6db5d85587857c3715e8d91a7dc8f4801c117fc89b0.png) 
and the vectors 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071281/assets/4fbbb82838d7fa94fe0aeb47ed48952bfe573e12874d3891f8650a15b46e0ee7.png)
Which of the given vectors belong to the kernel of $\mathbf{T}?$
e-5616.worked_solution:
A vector $\mathbf{u}$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ if $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{0}.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_i)$ for each vector $\mathbf v_i\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\,\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)=\mathbf{0},$ we conclude that, of the given vectors, the only vector that belongs to the kernel of $\,\mathbf{T}$ is $\,\mathbf{v}_1.$

content.knowledge_point: Determining Whether Given Vectors Belong to the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
content.problem:
Consider the linear transformation 
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}4x+2y \\ 6x+3y\end{aligned}]$ 
and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 6\end{aligned}],{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 6\end{aligned}].$
Which of the given vectors belong to the kernel of $T?$
content.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each vector ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 6\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 6\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\,T({v}_{2})=0,$ we conclude that the only vector that belongs to the kernel of $\,T$ is ${v}_{2}.$

content.knowledge_point: Determining Whether Given Vectors Belong to the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
content.problem:
Consider the linear transformation
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x+4y \\ y+z \\ x-4z\end{aligned}]$ and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Which of the given vectors belong to $\text{Ker}(T)?$
content.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})=T({v}_{3})=0,$ we conclude that the vectors that belong to the kernel of $T$ are ${v}_{1},$ ${v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}.$
